title: Given a number N (assume N >= 2), draw a flowchart to check whether it is prime and print Yes if prime, otherwise No. Start, read N, initialize i = 2 and isPrime = true, loop while i < N (or i*i <= N) doing if N % i == 0 then isPrime = false and break, i = i + 1, decision isPrime == true, Yes print Yes, No print No, End. Input: 7, Expected Output: Yes (e.g. 9 -> No).
shortTitle: Check Prime — check whether N is prime and print Yes or No

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A prime number is an integer greater than one that has no positive divisors other than one and itself. To test primality you try to divide N by each candidate factor starting at two; if any divides it evenly, N is composite, otherwise it is prime. The efficient version only tests candidates up to the square root of N, because if N has a factor larger than its square root it must also have a matching factor smaller than the square root.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India chooses prime numbers when configuring certain hashing and key parameters, because primes distribute values more evenly across buckets. To validate that a chosen parameter like seven is prime, the system checks whether any smaller number divides it evenly, finds none, and confirms it is prime. Nine, however, is divisible by three, so it is rejected.

**One line to remember:** A number is prime if no integer from two up to its square root divides it evenly, and checking only up to the square root is the key efficiency.

sections.s2_technical:
The basic algorithm sets a boolean isPrime to true and tries candidate divisors i starting at two. For each i it checks whether N modulo i equals zero; if so, i divides N evenly, N is composite, so isPrime becomes false and the loop can break immediately because one factor is enough to decide. If the loop finishes without finding a divisor, N is prime.

The crucial optimization is the loop bound. Testing i while i is less than N works but is wasteful. It is enough to test while i times i is less than or equal to N, that is up to the square root of N, because divisors come in pairs that multiply to N, and one member of each pair is always at or below the square root. So if no divisor is found up to the square root, none exists above it either. This changes the cost from linear in N to the square root of N, which is a huge saving for large values, and I always write the condition as `i * i <= n` to avoid computing a floating-point square root.

Edge handling matters: numbers below two are not prime by definition, two is the only even prime, and after checking two you could step i by two to skip even candidates for a further speedup. For the very large primes used in cryptographic key sizes, trial division is far too slow and you use probabilistic tests like Miller-Rabin, which is what BigInteger's isProbablePrime method does, and that is the senior-level choice for real key material. For small configuration parameters, the square-root trial-division loop shown here is correct and clear.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India validates that a configured hashing or key parameter is prime, because primes give better distribution. We must test primality of N. This is exactly the trial-division algorithm.

Problem 2 — Testing every divisor up to N would be slow for large parameters. This is exactly why the loop runs only up to the square root using i times i less than or equal to N.

Problem 3 — As soon as one divisor is found the answer is settled, so continuing wastes time. This is exactly why the loop breaks on the first divisor.

Our mini-project builds a `PrimeChecker` with an `isPrime(int n)` method using the square-root loop, and a `CheckPrimeDemo` runnable that confirms seven is prime and nine is not.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: N = 7 (and the composite case N = 9).

Step 1 — For seven, the check n less than two is false, so we proceed. The candidate divisor i starts at two.

Step 2 — The loop condition is i times i less than or equal to seven. Two times two is four, which is at most seven, so we test seven modulo two, which is one, not zero, so no divisor yet, and i becomes three.

Step 3 — Three times three is nine, which is greater than seven, so the loop condition fails and the loop ends without finding a divisor. Seven is therefore prime and the method returns true.

Step 4 — For nine, i starts at two, two times two is four at most nine, nine modulo two is one, no divisor, i becomes three. Three times three is nine, at most nine, and nine modulo three is zero, so three divides nine, the method returns false immediately.

Step 5 — The two results are logged: seven is prime with Yes, nine is not prime with No.

Final output:

```
2026-11-01 00:04:00 [INFO] Parameter 7 prime? Yes
2026-11-01 00:04:00 [INFO] Parameter 9 prime? No
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: N = 7
    │
    ▼
  i=2: i*i=4 <= 7 ? yes → 7%2=1 (no divisor) → i=3
  i=3: i*i=9 <= 7 ? no → stop
    │
    ▼
  no divisor found → PRIME → "Yes"

  Input: N = 9
  i=2: 9%2=1 → i=3
  i=3: i*i=9<=9 → 9%3=0 → divisor! → "No"
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Primality by Trial Division ═══

  ┌─ Principles ─────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: checker only decides primality            │
  │  Loop to sqrt(n) via i*i<=n → O(√N)           │
  │  Break on first divisor → stop early           │
  │  Big primes → BigInteger.isProbablePrime        │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │         PrimeChecker         │
  │ ──────────────────────────── │
  │ + isPrime(n: int): boolean   │
  └──────────────────────────────┘

  Contract for isPrime(n):
    Pre:  none (n<2 handled → false)
    Post: true iff n has no divisor in [2, √n]
    Note: for crypto-size use isProbablePrime

  Call Chain:
  1. isPrime(7)
  2.   i=2 → 7%2≠0
  3.   i=3 → 3*3>7 → stop
  4.   return true
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A prime number is an integer greater than one whose only positive divisors are one and itself. To test it, you try dividing N by each candidate factor starting at two, and if any divides it evenly the number is composite, otherwise it is prime. The flowchart sets a flag, loops the candidate divisor, sets the flag false and breaks on the first divisor it finds, and prints Yes or No based on the flag. Seven has no divisor, so it is prime, while nine is divisible by three, so it is not.

The key efficiency, and the thing an interviewer wants to hear, is that you only need to test candidate divisors up to the square root of N, not all the way to N. That is because divisors come in pairs that multiply to N, and at least one member of each pair is at or below the square root, so if nothing up to the square root divides N, nothing above it does either. I write that bound as i times i less than or equal to N to avoid a floating-point square root, and I break as soon as I find one divisor because a single factor settles the answer. That turns the cost from linear in N to the square root of N.

In my banking work at National Bank of India, I used this to validate configured hashing and key parameters, because prime moduli distribute values more evenly and reduce collisions. I wrote a PrimeChecker whose isPrime method does square-root trial division and short-circuits on the first divisor, treating anything below two as not prime. It confirmed seven and rejected nine. The important senior caveat I always add is that trial division is only appropriate for small configuration values, and for cryptographic-size primes you must use a probabilistic test such as the one behind BigInteger's isProbablePrime method, because trial division would be hopelessly slow at those sizes.
